Instability of the magnetohydrodynamics system at vanishing Reynolds number

Abstract

The aim of this note is to study the dynamo properties of the magnetohydrodynamics system at vanishing RmR_{m}. Improving the analysis in [6], we shall establish a generic Lyapunov instability result.

1 The induction equation

The incompressible Magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) system is a classical model for conducting fluids. It is derived from both Navier-Stokes equation for the fluid movement under the magnetic field and the Maxwell equations with Ohm’s law for the evolution of the magnetic field generated by the fluid movement. It is in dimensionless form:

{∂tu+u⋅∇u+∇p−1Re​Δ​u=(∇∧b)∧b+f,∂tb−∇∧(u∧b)−1Rm​Δ​b=0,∇⋅u=0,∇⋅b=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla p-\frac{1}{R_{e}}\Delta u=(\nabla\wedge b)\wedge b+f,\\ \partial_{t}b-\nabla\wedge(u\wedge b)-\frac{1}{R_{m}}\Delta b=0,\\ \nabla\cdot u=0,\\ \nabla\cdot b=0,\end{array}\right. (1)

where ReR_{e} and RmR_{m} are the hydrodynamic and magnetic Reynolds numbers. In this system, u=u⁡(t,θ)u=u(t,\theta) and b=b⁡(t,θ)b=b(t,\theta) are respectively the velocity field of the fluid and the magnetic field, vector-valued functions in \mb​R3\mb R^{3}, and ff is an additional forcing term (anything that is not the electromagnetic force). To lighten notations, we will assume in this note that Re=1R_{e}=1 and Rm=εR_{m}=\varepsilon, where ε\varepsilon is a small parameter. Note that the Reynolds magnetic number – that is the one that corresponds to the definition commonly used – is defined by Rm=L​VνmR_{m}=\frac{LV}{\nu_{m}}, where LL and VV are respectively the typical variation length and amplitude of the velocity field uu. This means that for a given time-and-space scale for the velocity field, we consider large magnetic diffusivity (or vanishing conductivity) of the fluid. The reader may refer to [3] to have a complete explanation on how the above MHD system is computed. One may say it is the base system for describing MHD in the case of a conducting viscous fluid.

Our aim here, related to dynamo theory is to deal with the stability of solutions of this last system, and more precisely with the instability of solutions of the form

(u,b)=(u⁡(t,x),0).(u,b)=(u(t,x),0). (2)

The physical problem behind the study of the stability of such solutions is to understand the generation of magnetic field by the fluid. The fluid “gives” energy to the magnetic field by the term ∇∧(u∧b)\nabla\wedge(u\wedge b), which should compensate the dissipation term in the equation. We know for long that this kind of phenomena occurs in planets and stars like the Sun or the Earth and make them act like a magnet (See [9] where the problem was first posed).

There have been many results in the past century in dynamo theory. First results where “negative” results in the sense that they gave condition for which fluids cannot generate a dynamo effect, i.e. this corresponds to situations where solutions of the form (2) were actually stable. Those results spread the idea that the velocity field has to be chaotic enough to expect a dynamo effect (See M.M.Vishik, [16]). The knowledge in the domain concerning stability of the MHD system has been summed up in [7].

Then positive results began to emerge concerning kinetic dynamos, that is a dynamo where we consider only the induction equation in the system: physically, this corresponds to the case where the Laplace force is neglected in the fluid movement, i.e. the magnetic field has no retro-action on the fluid. This case is much simpler since it corresponds to only a linear case. More recent results gave positive result with the full MHD system, which is non-linear.

In this note, we will focus on a particular mechanism for the generation of magnetic field, that is the “alpha-effect”, which was first introduced by E.N. Parker [11]. This mechanism is based on scale separation: we formally decompose the fields into two parts, a fluctuating one, evolving on small lengths, and a mean one evolving on much bigger ones. The idea is that the small-scale field can have an effect on the big-scale one through the mean part of the crossed-term ∇∧(u∧b)\nabla\wedge(u\wedge b) in the induction equation and may create instability on the large-scale. Note that this kind of mechanism has been experimentally confirmed much recently by R. Stieglitz and U. Müller [14].

Three regimes of RmR_{m} can be identified in the MHD system:

The intermediate regime where RmR_{m} is of order 11.

We considered this regime in a former article [2].

The regime of large RmR_{m}.

In that case, one can expect a dynamo at the scale of the velocity field, since the diffusive effect is very weak at such scale. A related question is whether the dynamo is “fast” or “slow”, that is whether the best growing mode decreases to 00 as \tend​Rm+∞\tend{R_{m}}{+\infty} or not. So far this regime has been mainly studied formally and numerically (up to Rm∼105R_{m}\sim 10^{5}) in physics [10, 13, 12, 1], in particular in the case of ABC-like flows, and the result seems to be difficult to predict in the considered cases. This regime will be the object of a forthcoming paper.

The regime of small RmR_{m}.

This regime is relevant to laboratory experiments, and is the focus of the present note. More precisely, we use the α\alpha-effect mechanism to obtain a linearized instability result for system (1), around steady states (u,b)=(U⁡(θ),0)(u,b)=(U(\theta),0). Then, we conclude to a Lyapunov instability result for the full non-linear system.

The base flows we consider satisfy

U∈\mc​H∞​(\mb​T3)3U\in\mc H^{\infty}(\mb T^{3})^{3} (3)

and

∫\mb​T3U=0, and∇θ⋅U=0.\int_{\mb T^{3}}U=0,\text{ and}\qquad\nabla_{\theta}\cdot U=0. (4)

We denote by \ms​P\ms P the set of fields UU of this form. \ms​P\ms P is a Fréchet space for the associated semi-norms

‖U‖m2=∑ξ∈\mb​Z4|ξ|2​m​|U^​(ξ)|2.\|U\|_{m}^{2}=\sum_{\xi\in\mb Z^{4}}|\xi|^{2m}|\hat{U}(\xi)|^{2}. (5)

We have

u=U+u′,b=0+b′,u=U+u^{\prime},\quad b=0+b^{\prime}, (6)

focusing on the growth of the perturbations u′,b′u^{\prime},b^{\prime}. As we shall see, it is also convenient to do a rescaling in time: t′=ε3​tt^{\prime}=\varepsilon^{3}t. Dropping the primes, we end up with:

{∂tb−ε−3∇∧(U∧b)−ε−3∇∧(u∧b)−ε−4Δb=0,ε3​∂tu+u⋅∇U+U⋅∇u+u⋅∇u+∇p−Δ​u=(∇∧b)∧b∇⋅b=0∇⋅u=0\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{t}b-\varepsilon^{-3}\nabla\wedge(U\wedge b)-\varepsilon^{-3}\nabla\wedge(u\wedge b)-\varepsilon^{-4}\Delta b=0,\\ \varepsilon^{3}\partial_{t}u+u\cdot\nabla U+U\cdot\nabla u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla p-\Delta u=(\nabla\wedge b)\wedge b\\ \nabla\cdot b=0\\ \nabla\cdot u=0\end{array}\right. (7)

As mentioned before, a key point is the understanding of the linearized induction equation,

∂tb−ε−3∇∧(U∧b)−ε−4Δb=0,\partial_{t}b-\varepsilon^{-3}\nabla\wedge(U\wedge b)-\varepsilon^{-4}\Delta b=0, (8)

Motivated by the analysis of the α\alpha-effect, we will look for an exponentially growing solution of that equation based on scale separation:

bε​(t,θ)=eλε​t​(b¯​(ε2​θ)+ε​b~​(ε2​θ,θ)),b^{\varepsilon}(t,\theta)=e^{\lambda^{\varepsilon}t}(\bar{b}(\varepsilon^{2}\theta)+\varepsilon\tilde{b}(\varepsilon^{2}\theta,\theta)), (9)

where b¯=b¯​(x)\bar{b}=\bar{b}(x) and b~=b~​(x,θ)\tilde{b}=\tilde{b}(x,\theta) depend on the original small-scale variable θ\theta, but also on a large-scale variable x=ε2​θx=\varepsilon^{2}\theta. In this decomposition, b~∈\mc​Hlocs​(\mb​R3×\mb​T3)\tilde{b}\in\mc H_{\text{loc}}^{s}(\mb R^{3}\times\mb T^{3}) is periodic and average-free with respect to the second variable θ\theta, whereas b¯∈\mc​Hlocs​(\mb​R3)\bar{b}\in\mc H_{\text{loc}}^{s}(\mb R^{3}).

Using the formal variable separation above, the equation then writes under the form

ε​λε​b~+λε​b¯−∇x∧(U∧b~)−1ε​∇x∧(U∧b¯)−1ε2​∇θ∧(U∧b~)−1ε3​∇θ∧(U∧b¯)−1ε3​Δθ​b~−ε​Δx​b~−Δx​b¯−2ε​∑i=13∂xi​θib~=0.\begin{split}\varepsilon\lambda^{\varepsilon}\tilde{b}&+\lambda^{\varepsilon}\bar{b}-\nabla_{x}\wedge(U\wedge\tilde{b})-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\nabla_{x}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})-\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\tilde{b})\\ &-\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})-\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}\Delta_{\theta}\tilde{b}-\varepsilon\Delta_{x}\tilde{b}-\Delta_{x}\bar{b}-\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_{x_{i}\theta_{i}}\tilde{b}=0.\end{split} (10)

We split this equation between mean part and fluctuating part:

Δθ​b~+ε​∇θ∧(U∧b~)+∇θ∧(U∧b¯)+ε2​(∇x⋅∇θ+∇θ⋅∇x)​b~+ε2​∇x∧(U∧b¯)+ε3​∇x∧(U∧b~)~+ε4​Δx​b~=ε4​λε​b~,\begin{split}\Delta_{\theta}\tilde{b}&+\varepsilon\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\tilde{b})+\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})+\varepsilon^{2}(\nabla_{x}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}+\nabla_{\theta}\cdot\nabla_{x})\tilde{b}+\\ &\varepsilon^{2}\nabla_{x}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})+\varepsilon^{3}\nabla_{x}\wedge\widetilde{(U\wedge\tilde{b})}+\varepsilon^{4}\Delta_{x}\tilde{b}=\varepsilon^{4}\lambda^{\varepsilon}\tilde{b},\end{split} (11)

And we rewrite the fluctuating part of the equation to separate terms with b~\tilde{b} and b¯\bar{b}:

Δθ​b~+ε​∇θ∧(U∧b~)+ε2​(∇x⋅∇θ+∇θ⋅∇x)​b~+ε3​∇x∧(U∧b~)~+ε4​Δx​b~−ε4​λε​b~=−∇θ∧(U∧b¯)−ε2​∇x∧(U∧b¯)\begin{split}\Delta_{\theta}\tilde{b}&+\varepsilon\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\tilde{b})+\varepsilon^{2}(\nabla_{x}\cdot\nabla_{\theta}+\nabla_{\theta}\cdot\nabla_{x})\tilde{b}+\varepsilon^{3}\nabla_{x}\wedge\widetilde{(U\wedge\tilde{b})}+\varepsilon^{4}\Delta_{x}\tilde{b}-\varepsilon^{4}\lambda^{\varepsilon}\tilde{b}\\ &=-\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})-\varepsilon^{2}\nabla_{x}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})\end{split} (13)

Equations (11) to (13) will be used extensively throughout the note.

We can now give the theorems that we will prove in this note. The first one is related to the induction equation (8): {theoreme} Let s>0s>0 be a real number. There exists a dense subset Ω\Omega of \ms​P\ms P such that for all U∈ΩU\in\Omega, there exists a real ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0, a vector ξ∈\mb​R3\xi\in\mb R^{3} and a function \fonctionλU[[0,ε0[][\mbR+∗]\fonction{\lambda_{U}}[[0,\varepsilon_{0}[][\mb R_{+}^{*}] analytic such that for all ε∈[0,ε0[\varepsilon\in[0,\varepsilon_{0}[, there exists a solution bb of (8) of the form:

bε​(θ,t)=eλU​(ε)​t+ε2​\iim​ξ⋅θ​(b¯′+ε​b~′​(θ)),b^{\varepsilon}(\theta,t)=e^{\lambda_{U}(\varepsilon)t+\varepsilon^{2}\iim\xi\cdot\theta}(\bar{b}^{\prime}+\varepsilon\tilde{b}^{\prime}(\theta)), (14)

where U∈\ms​PU\in\ms P, b¯′∈\mb​R3\bar{b}^{\prime}\in\mb R^{3} and b~′∈\mc​H0s​(\mb​T3)\tilde{b}^{\prime}\in\mc H_{0}^{s}(\mb T^{3}). Our second theorem concerns the full MHD system (7). For this next theorem, we introduce for any vector T∈(\mb​R+∗)3T\in(\mb R_{+}^{*})^{3} the Sobolev space \mc​HTs=\mc​Hs​(\mb​R/T1​\mb​Z×\mb​R/T2​\mb​Z×\mb​R/T3​\mb​Z)\mc H^{s}_{T}=\mc H^{s}(\mb R/T_{1}\mb Z\times\mb R/T_{2}\mb Z\times\mb R/T_{3}\mb Z) {theoreme} Suppose s>3/2+1s>3/2+1. Then there exists a dense subset Ω\Omega of \ms​P\ms P such that for all U∈ΩU\in\Omega, there exists a vector T=(T1,T2,T3)T=(T_{1},T_{2},T_{3}) with integer coordinates and a sequence (εn)n≥0(\varepsilon_{n})_{n\geq 0} decreasing to 00 such that the solution (U0)\begin{pmatrix}U\\ 0\end{pmatrix} of the (MHD) system (1) is nonlinearly unstable in \mc​HTs\mc H_{T}^{s} in the following sense:

There exists initial values

(u0b0)∈\mc​HTs,\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix}\in\mc H_{T}^{s}, (15)

and C0>0C_{0}>0 such that for all δ>0\delta>0, the solution (uδbδ)\begin{pmatrix}u_{\delta}\\ b_{\delta}\end{pmatrix} of (7) with initial value δ​(u0b0)\delta\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix} satisfies

‖(uδbδ)⁡(tδ)‖\mc​HTs≥C0\left\|\begin{pmatrix}u_{\delta}\\ b_{\delta}\end{pmatrix}(t_{\delta})\right\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}\geq C_{0} (16)

for some time tδt_{\delta}.

This result extends substantially the article [6] by D. Gérard-Varet. Recast in our variables, this article considers the case of large magnetic diffusion, that is Rm=ε≪1R_{m}=\varepsilon\ll 1. Let us point out that D. Gérard-Varet didn’t use the physicists scaling for the velocity field, thus making possible confusion to the fact that he chose « Rm=1R_{m}=1 » and that it actually corresponds to the case where RmR_{m} is vanishing with ε\varepsilon. To get the usual Reynolds number you have to do a time-space transformation t↦t/ε3t\mapsto t/\varepsilon^{3}, x↦x/ε2x\mapsto x/\varepsilon^{2} (and multiply the amplitude VV by 1/ε1/\varepsilon), thus making the Reynolds number ε\varepsilon instead of 11.

Briefly, it is shown in [6] that for all m∈\mb​Nm\in\mb N, there are solutions of (8) (on a larger box depending on ε\varepsilon) that go from amplitude εm\varepsilon^{m} initially to an amplitude η=η⁡(m)>0\eta=\eta(m)>0 independent of ε\varepsilon (but depending on mm). Note that, as η\eta depends on mm, the result in [6] does not yield Lyapunov instability at fixed small ε\varepsilon, contrary to ours.

The main idea to prove our two theorems is to construct an exact solution (b¯,b~)(\bar{b},\tilde{b}) of equations (11) to (13). We shall obtain it through a perturbative argument, starting from the case ε=0\varepsilon=0.

2 Case ε=0\varepsilon=0

2.1 An eigenvalue problem

The fluctuating part in the case ε=0\varepsilon=0 is

Δθ​b~=−∇θ∧(U∧b¯).\Delta_{\theta}\tilde{b}=-\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b}). (17)

Since the Laplacian is invertible as a function from \mc​H0s+2\mc H_{0}^{s+2} to \mc​H0s\mc H_{0}^{s}, we can write

b~=−Δθ−1​∇θ∧(U∧b¯)=\ms​L​(θ)​b¯,\tilde{b}=-\Delta_{\theta}^{-1}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})=\ms L(\theta)\bar{b}, (18)

where \fonction​\ms​L​(θ)​\mc​H0s​\mc​H0s+1\fonction{\ms L(\theta)}{\mc H_{0}^{s}}{\mc H_{0}^{s+1}} (xx can be taken as a parameter since it is not involved in \ms​L\ms L).

Now we can replace b~\tilde{b} by \ms​L​(θ)​b¯\ms L(\theta)\bar{b} in the mean part of the equation (12) to have an equation involving only b¯\bar{b}:

∇x∧U∧\ms​L​(θ)​b¯¯+Δx​b¯=λ0​b¯.\nabla_{x}\wedge\overline{U\wedge\ms L(\theta)\bar{b}}+\Delta_{x}\bar{b}=\lambda^{0}\bar{b}. (19)

We introduce the matrix α\alpha defined by

α(U)b¯=U∧\ms​L​(θ)​b¯¯=−∫[0,1]3U∧Δθ−1∇θ∧(U∧b¯)\udθ.\alpha(U)\bar{b}=\overline{U\wedge\ms L(\theta)\bar{b}}=-\int_{[0,1]^{3}}U\wedge\Delta_{\theta}^{-1}\nabla_{\theta}\wedge(U\wedge\bar{b})\ud\theta. (20)

(The name of the matrix is the one related to the so called alpha effect mentionned in the introduction)

Now the equation is

∇x∧(α⁡(U)​b¯)+Δx​b¯=λ0​b¯.\nabla_{x}\wedge(\alpha(U)\bar{b})+\Delta_{x}\bar{b}=\lambda^{0}\bar{b}. (21)

We will find a solution of this last equation under the form b¯​(x)=e\iim​ξ⋅x​b¯′\bar{b}(x)=e^{\iim\xi\cdot x}\bar{b}^{\prime}. Using this stanza, the equation then has the form (dropping the prime to lighten notations in the end of the subsection):

\iim​ξ∧(α⁡(U)​b¯)−|ξ|2​b¯=λ0​b¯.\iim\xi\wedge(\alpha(U)\bar{b})-|\xi|^{2}\bar{b}=\lambda^{0}\bar{b}. (22)

Thus we have come now to an eigenvalue problem with the matrix ξ∧α⁡(U)\xi\wedge\alpha(U). The properties of the matrix α\alpha are the source of the alpha-effect mechanism; they have been already studied in [6] and in [2] with a more general case. We give here a proposition which is only the particular case of the similar study done in those papers:

{proposition}

The matrix α⁡(U)\alpha(U) defined above is real and symmetric. Furthermore, there exists a dense subset Ω\Omega of \ms​P\ms P such that for all profile U∈ΩU\in\Omega, there exists some ξ∈\mb​R3\xi\in\mb R^{3} such that the matrix defined by the left hand side of (22) admits an eigenvalue of positive real part. The reader should refer to those paper for a proof of this proposition.

From now on, we will assume that our base flow belongs to this subset Ω\Omega. This gives the existence of a vector ξ∈\mb​R3\xi\in\mb R^{3} and an eigenvector b0b_{0} associated to an eigenvalue λ0\lambda^{0} with positive real part such that

b¯​(x)=e\iim​ξ⋅x​b0\bar{b}(x)=e^{\iim\xi\cdot x}b_{0} (23)

is a growing mode of (21)

where the matrix α\alpha depends here on some parameters:

det(\iim​ξ∧αξ,ε,λε​(u)−|ξ|2​\Id−λε​\Id)=0,\det(\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\lambda^{\varepsilon}}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\lambda^{\varepsilon}\Id)=0, (31)

\iim​ξ∧αξ,ε,λε​(u)=\iim​(0−ξ3ξ2ξ30−ξ1−ξ2ξ10)​αξ,ε,λε​(u)=Aξ​αξ,ε,λε​(u).\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\lambda^{\varepsilon}}(u)=\iim\begin{pmatrix}0&-\xi_{3}&\xi_{2}\\ \xi_{3}&0&-\xi_{1}\\ -\xi_{2}&\xi_{1}&0\end{pmatrix}\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\lambda^{\varepsilon}}(u)=A^{\xi}\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\lambda^{\varepsilon}}(u). f⁡(ε,μ)=det(\iim​ξ∧αξ,ε,μ​(u)−|ξ|2​\Id−μ​\Id),f(\varepsilon,\mu)=\det(\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\mu}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\mu\Id), (33)

4 Implicit function theorem

We know from former section that f⁡(0,λ0)=0f(0,\lambda^{0})=0. Now we want to prove that for ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, there exists λε\lambda^{\varepsilon} such that f⁡(ε,λε)=0f(\varepsilon,\lambda^{\varepsilon})=0. Furthermore, ff is analytic in (ε,μ)(\varepsilon,\mu) in VV.

We prove in this section that ∂f∂μ|ε=0μ=λ0≠0\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mu}\right|_{\begin{subarray}{l}\varepsilon=0\\ \mu=\lambda^{0}\end{subarray}}\neq 0, so that we can apply the analytic implicit functions theorem and conclude that there exists a neighborhood WW of 00 and a function \fonction​φ​W​\mb​R\fonction{\varphi}{W}{\mb R} such that φ⁡(0)=λ0\varphi(0)=\lambda^{0} and ∀ε∈W,f⁡(ε,φ⁡(ε))=0\forall\varepsilon\in W,f(\varepsilon,\varphi(\varepsilon))=0 (we can then restrict this neighborhood to positive values of ε\varepsilon).

We compute now ∂f∂μ|ε=0μ=λ0\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mu}\right|_{\begin{subarray}{l}\varepsilon=0\\ \mu=\lambda^{0}\end{subarray}}: using usual computation rules on composition of functions, we have that

∂f∂μ|ε=0μ=λ0=\uddet|\iim​ξ∧αξ,0,λ0​(u)−|ξ|2​\Id−λ0​\Id∘\ud(\iimξ∧αξ,ε,μ(u)−|ξ|2\Id−μ\Id)|ε=0μ=λ0(0,1).\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mu}\right|_{\begin{subarray}{l}\varepsilon=0\\ \mu=\lambda^{0}\end{subarray}}=\left.\ud\det\right|_{\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,0,\lambda^{0}}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\lambda^{0}\Id}\circ\left.\ud(\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\mu}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\mu\Id)\right|_{\begin{subarray}{l}\varepsilon=0\\ \mu=\lambda^{0}\end{subarray}}(0,1). (34)

The computation of the second differential is straightforward and gives

\ud​(\iim​ξ∧αξ,ε,μ​(u)−|ξ|2​\Id−μ​\Id)|ε=0μ=λ0​(0,1)=∂(\iim​ξ∧αξ,ε,μ​(u)−|ξ|2​\Id−μ​\Id)∂μ|ε=0μ=λ0=−\Id.\left.\ud(\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\mu}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\mu\Id)\right|_{\begin{subarray}{l}\varepsilon=0\\ \mu=\lambda^{0}\end{subarray}}(0,1)=\left.\frac{\partial(\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,\varepsilon,\mu}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\mu\Id)}{\partial\mu}\right|_{\begin{subarray}{l}\varepsilon=0\\ \mu=\lambda^{0}\end{subarray}}=-\Id. (35)

And the computation of the first one gives

\uddet|\iim​ξ∧αξ,0,λ0​(u)−|ξ|2​\Id−λ0​\Id(−\Id)=−\Tr(\com(\iimξ∧αξ,0,λ0(u)−|ξ|2\Id−λ0\Id)).\left.\ud\det\right|_{\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,0,\lambda^{0}}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\lambda^{0}\Id}(-\Id)=-\Tr(\com(\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,0,\lambda^{0}}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\lambda^{0}\Id)). (36)

We know from the second section the matrix A=\iim​ξ∧αξ,0,λ0​(u)−|ξ|2​\Id−λ0​\IdA=\iim\xi\wedge\alpha_{\xi,0,\lambda^{0}}(u)-|\xi|^{2}\Id-\lambda^{0}\Id is diagonalizable and that his eigenvalues are 0,−λ0,−2​λ00,-\lambda^{0},-2\lambda^{0}. Thus, \com​(A)\com(A) is similar to the matrix

\com​(0000−λ0000−2​λ0)=(2​(λ0)200000000),\com\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\ 0&-\lambda^{0}&0\\ 0&0&-2\lambda^{0}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2(\lambda^{0})^{2}&0&0\\ 0&0&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}, (37)

which is of trace 2​(λ0)2≠02(\lambda^{0})^{2}\neq 0.

Thus

∂f∂μ|ε=0μ=λ0=2​(λ0)2≠0.\left.\frac{\partial f}{\partial\mu}\right|_{\begin{subarray}{l}\varepsilon=0\\ \mu=\lambda^{0}\end{subarray}}=2(\lambda^{0})^{2}\neq 0. (38)

Since φ\varphi is continuous on 00, and φ⁡(0)=λ0\varphi(0)=\lambda^{0} has positive real value, this remains true for ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, which concludes the proof of the existence of a growing mode for a small ε>0\varepsilon>0.

5 Nonlinear instability

We will now prove nonlinear instability of the system (8). For that we will adapt a method developped by S. Friedlander, W. Strauss and M. Vishik in [5] (itself adapted from Y. Guo and W. Strauss in [8]) to prove nonlinear instability given linear instability. The condition s>3/2+1s>3/2+1 in the main theorem is used only in this section to obtain an inequality on the nonlinear terms similar to that in the article [5]. Actually, using the parabolic feature of the MHD system, it would be possible to lower our regularity requirements (see for instance Friedlander et al [4] in the context of the Navier-Stokes equations). We stick here to regular data for simplicity of exposure.

Let U∈\ms​PU\in\ms P belonging to the dense subset of linearly unstable flows described in the previous section.

We introduce Leray operator \mb​P\mb P to get rid of pp. We rewrite system (7) as

∂t\ms​U+Ls​\ms​U=Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U),\partial_{t}\ms U+L_{s}\ms U=Q(\ms U,\ms U), (39)

where

\ms​U=(u′b),\ms U=\begin{pmatrix}u^{\prime}\\ b\end{pmatrix}, (40)
Ls​\ms​U=ε−3​(\mb​P​(u⋅∇u′+u′⋅∇u)−Δ​u′−∇∧(u∧b)−Δb)L_{s}\ms U=\varepsilon^{-3}\begin{pmatrix}\mb P(u\cdot\nabla u^{\prime}+u^{\prime}\cdot\nabla u)-\Delta u^{\prime}\\ -\nabla\wedge(u\wedge b)-\Delta b\end{pmatrix} (41)

is the linearized operator around (u0)\begin{pmatrix}u\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, and

Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U)=ε−3​(\mb​P​((∇∧b)∧b−u′⋅∇u′)∇∧(u′∧b))Q(\ms U,\ms U)=\varepsilon^{-3}\begin{pmatrix}\mb P((\nabla\wedge b)\wedge b-u^{\prime}\cdot\nabla u^{\prime})\\ \nabla\wedge(u^{\prime}\wedge b)\end{pmatrix} (42)

is the nonlinearity.

We shall consider this system in \mc​HTs\mc H_{T}^{s}, TT to be specified later. We also denote LT2=\mc​HT0L^{2}_{T}=\mc H_{T}^{0} the L2L^{2} space on the torus. Since we will work in these spaces until the end of the proof, we will drop the TT in the notation. We have the following a priori estimates for the nonlinear term:

Every term of every component of Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U)Q(\ms U,\ms U) can be written as a product of one component of \ms​U\ms U and one of ∇\msU\nabla\ms U (composed by \mb​P\mb P). Thus, we have the first estimate

∥Q(\msU,\msU)∥L2≤Cε−3∥|\msU||∇\msU|∥L2≤Cε−3∥\msU∥L2∥∇\msU∥L∞.\|Q(\ms U,\ms U)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\varepsilon^{-3}\||\ms U||\nabla\ms U|\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\varepsilon^{-3}\|\ms U\|_{L^{2}}\|\nabla\ms U\|_{L^{\infty}}. (43)

For r=12​(s+n/2+1)>n/2+1r=\frac{1}{2}(s+n/2+1)>n/2+1 (here n=3n=3), we have that

∥∇\msU∥L∞≤∥\msU∥\mc​Hr,\|\nabla\ms U\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{r}}, (44)

and

‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hr≤C​‖\ms​U‖L2η​‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hs1−η\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{r}}\leq C\|\ms U\|_{L^{2}}^{\eta}\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{s}}^{1-\eta} (45)

for η\eta such that r=(1−η)​sr=(1-\eta)s (i.e. η=12−n+24​s=12−54​s\eta=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{n+2}{4s}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4s}).

Thus, we have:

‖Q⁡(\ms​U,\ms​U)‖L2≤C​ε−3​‖\ms​U‖L21+η​‖\ms​U‖\mc​Hs1−η\|Q(\ms U,\ms U)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\varepsilon^{-3}\|\ms U\|_{L^{2}}^{1+\eta}\|\ms U\|_{\mc H^{s}}^{1-\eta} (46)

We shall prove the following theorem, which is a mere reformulation of the second theorem: {theoreme} Suppose s>3/2+1s>3/2+1. Then there exists a vector T=(T1,T2,T3)T=(T_{1},T_{2},T_{3}) with integer coordinates and a sequence (εn)n≥0(\varepsilon_{n})_{n\geq 0} decreasing to 00 such that the system (39) is nonlinearly unstable in \mc​HTs\mc H_{T}^{s} in the following sense:

There exists a growing mode \ms​U0=(u0b0)\ms U_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix} with ‖\ms​U0‖\mc​HTs=1\|\ms U_{0}\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}=1 of the linearized system and a constant C0>0C_{0}>0 depending only on \ms​U0,s,n,ρ\ms U_{0},s,n,\rho such that for all δ>0\delta>0, the solution of the full magnetohydrodynamics system with initial value δ​\ms​U0\delta\ms U_{0} satisfies ‖\ms​U​(tδ)‖\mc​HTs≥C0\|\ms U(t_{\delta})\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}\geq C_{0} for some time tδt_{\delta}. {remarque} This theorem only proves that the solution reaches high values in finite time no matter how small the initial condition is. In particular it doesn’t say wether it explodes in finite time or is defined for all time, since both situations are possible in the result of the theorem. Actually, for small enough initial data (that is small enough δ\delta), it is classical that the solution of the system doesn’t explode in finite time. More details in [15] (Theorem 3.8)

Assume in contrary that the system is nonlinearly stable while spectrally unstable, that is that for any growing mode of initial value \ms​U0=(u0b0)\ms U_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ b_{0}\end{pmatrix} with ‖\ms​U0‖\mc​HTs=1\|\ms U_{0}\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}=1 in any box TT of the system (i.e. an eigenvector of LsL_{s} associated to an eigenvalue with positive real part) and for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a δ>0\delta>0 such that for all t>0t>0, the solution \ms​U​(t)\ms U(t) of the system with initial values δ​\ms​U0\delta\ms U_{0} satisfies ‖\ms​U​(t)‖\mc​HTs≤ε\|\ms U(t)\|_{\mc H_{T}^{s}}\leq\varepsilon.
